No imagination could picture how overwhelming the same sight would have been in the darkness of night. Hell itself might have been a suitable comparison. Even in daylight, my hair stood on end as I stared far down into those enormous openings. I imagined myself descending and wandering through their strange vaulted chambers, their glowing depths, and the dreadful red chasms of that hideous, bottomless fire. My escape had been narrow indeed. If the balloon had stayed inside the cloud just a little longer—if getting wet had not made me decide to throw out the ballast—I would certainly have been destroyed. Though people rarely consider them, such dangers may be the greatest faced by anyone travelling in a balloon. By now, however, I had risen too high to worry about that danger any longer.

‘I was climbing quickly, and by seven o’clock the barometer showed that I was at least nine and a half miles high. Breathing had become very difficult. My head also hurt terribly. For some time I had felt dampness on my cheeks; at last I discovered that it was blood, flowing quite rapidly from my eardrums. My eyes troubled me greatly too. When I passed my hand over them, they seemed to be bulging a considerable distance from their sockets. Everything in the basket, and even the balloon itself, looked distorted. These symptoms were worse than I had expected and began to frighten me. At this point, foolishly and without thinking, I tossed three five-pound weights out of the basket. This made the balloon rise faster, carrying me too suddenly into a layer of very thin air, without enough time to adjust. The result nearly ended both my journey and my life. A sudden spasm seized me and lasted more than five minutes. Even when it eased somewhat, I could only draw gasping breaths at long intervals. All the while, blood poured from my nose and ears, and even a little from my eyes. The pigeons seemed to be suffering terribly and struggled to escape. The cat cried pitifully, staggering back and forth in the basket with her tongue hanging out, as though she had been poisoned. Too late, I realised how reckless I had been to throw out the ballast, and I became desperately agitated. I expected nothing but death, and death within a few minutes.

Should I go and see them? Or Miss Bates? She is even closer. And I’m not sure anyone would understand what the others want better than Miss Bates. I do think we need more people to advise us. Suppose I invite her to join us?’

‘Well, if you like,’ Mrs. Weston said with some hesitation, ‘if you think she can help.’

‘You won’t get anything useful out of Miss Bates,’ Emma said. ‘She will be full of delight and gratitude, but she will tell you nothing. She won’t even listen to your questions. I see no benefit in consulting her.’

‘But she is so entertaining—so extremely entertaining! I love listening to Miss Bates talk. And I don’t have to bring the entire family, you know.’

Mr. Weston joined them just then and, hearing the proposal, gave it his firm approval.

‘Yes, do, Frank. Go and bring Miss Bates, and let’s settle the matter. I’m sure she will enjoy the idea, and I can’t think of anyone better at showing us how to resolve difficulties. Fetch Miss Bates. We are becoming rather too particular. She is a constant example of how to be happy. But bring them both. Invite both of them.’

‘Both, sir? Would the old lady be able to—?’

‘The old lady! No, the young lady, of course. I shall think you a complete fool, Frank, if you bring the aunt without her niece.’

‘Oh, forgive me, sir. I didn’t think of her immediately. Certainly, if you wish, I will try to persuade them both.’ And off he ran.

Long before he returned with the small, neat, quick-moving aunt and her elegant niece, Mrs. Weston had behaved like the good-natured woman and good wife she was: she examined the passage again and found its disadvantages much smaller than she had first thought—quite trivial, in fact. That settled the difficult decisions. Everything else, in theory at least, went perfectly smoothly. The lesser arrangements for tables and chairs, lighting and music, tea and supper seemed to settle themselves, or were left as minor details for Mrs. Weston and Mrs. Stokes to work out whenever they liked. Everyone invited was certain to attend. Frank had already written to Enscombe asking to extend his fortnight’s visit by a few days, a request that could not possibly be refused. The dance would be delightful.

When Miss Bates arrived, she agreed with the greatest warmth that it must be. They no longer needed her advice, but her approval—a far safer role—was most welcome. Her praise, embracing both the whole plan and every detail, warm and unending, could hardly fail to please. For another half-hour they walked between the rooms, some making suggestions, others listening, and everyone happily anticipating the occasion.

And he always pretended that Peter had written him all those things, but that was a lie. He’d picked up every last one from the young fool we’d taken out to the steamboat in the canoe.

Then Mary Jane brought the letter her father had left, and the king read it aloud and cried over it. It left the house and three thousand dollars in gold to the girls. Harvey and William were to get the tannery, which was doing good business, along with other houses and land worth about seven thousand, plus three thousand dollars in gold. The letter also said where the six thousand in cash was hidden in the cellar. So the two cheats announced that they would fetch it and make everything open and aboveboard, and told me to bring a candle. We closed the cellar door behind us. When they found the bag, they poured it onto the floor, and all those gold coins made a beautiful sight. My, how the king’s eyes shone! He slapped the duke’s shoulder and said:

‘Oh, this isn’t wonderful or anything! No, I should think not! Why, Bilji, it beats the Nonesuch, doesn’t it?’

The duke agreed. They grabbed handfuls of gold, sifted the coins between their fingers, and let them fall jingling to the floor. Then the king said:

‘There’s no question about it: being brothers to a rich dead man, and acting for heirs abroad who’ve been left money, is the business for you and me, Bilge. This is what comes of trusting Providence. It pays best in the long run. I’ve tried every way, and nothing beats it.’

Most people would have been satisfied with that heap and accepted the amount on trust. But these two had to count it. So they counted, and it came to four hundred and fifteen dollars less than it should. The king said:

‘Damn him, what did he do with that four hundred and fifteen dollars?’

They puzzled over it for a while and searched everywhere. Then the duke said:

‘Well, he was a very sick man and probably made a mistake. I reckon that explains it. Best to leave it alone and say nothing. We can afford the loss.’

‘Oh, sure, we can afford it. That isn’t what bothers me—it’s the amount. We want to look completely honest and open here, you know. We want to carry this money upstairs and count it in front of everyone, so there’s nothing to raise suspicion. But if the dead man says there’s six thousand dollars, you see, we don’t want to—’
